findings.where: Screen 6 worked-example note (WK_NOTE) and the Keep this rule line
findings.what: "1.5 to 2.5 U0 is common practice" is an unsourced claim: the only source is his notes, which give 1.5 to 2.5 U0 as the range for installation, acceptance and maintenance and say nothing about how common it is; say it plainly, e.g. "One range in use is 1.5 to 2.5 U0. IEEE puts installation and acceptance from under 2 U0 up to 3 U0."

findings.where: Screen 7, text after 5(a) is answered (SPEC[i5A].after), and the practice list
findings.what: "Above 35 kV, the cable ends may need terminations fitted..." drops the word "rated" from the source ("cables rated above 35 kV"), so it reads as a test-voltage threshold, and it sits beside the near-identical 36 kV resonant-test threshold on screen 2 and the card; write "On a cable rated above 35 kV, the ends may need terminations fitted to stop flashover."

findings.where: Screen 2, What it is for, second paragraph
findings.what: "Take a defect big enough to be excited at the test voltage." uses the source's jargon "excited", so a tired reader has to read it twice; rewrite as "Take a defect bad enough to spark at the test voltage."

"25.21 mA is all the set must supply. That is 76 × 0.02521 = 1.92 kVA." says a current "is" a power, and "all" ignores the leakage the lesson admits it leaves out; write "At 76 kV the set supplies 76 × 0.02521 = 1.92 kVA."

"DC withstand tests on XLPE cable are now discouraged." is passive with no one doing the discouraging, and the two sentences before it both start "That", so the second "That" (space charge speeding up water trees) reads ambiguously; write "Standards now discourage DC withstand tests on XLPE." and "This trapped charge can speed up water trees in healthy XLPE."

findings.where: Screen 1, Do you still have it?
findings.what: The question hands him the 1.5 to 2.5 U0 multiples, so it tests only U0 against the line voltage, not whether he still has the range; the brief asked for the range from memory, so asking "What VLF test voltage range applies to a 12/20 kV cable?" (same three choices) would make Skip to the practice a truer test.

String B is 66 kV, above the 36 kV where screen 2 says a submarine cable's spec may ask for a 10 to 500 Hz resonant test, but the setup never connects the two; add one sentence such as "String B is above 36 kV, so a real spec may ask for a resonant test. Here it asks for VLF."

"At 0.1 Hz the core is filled and emptied once in 10 s" undercounts the cycle the paragraph above describes (fill, empty, fill the other way, empty); say "charged one way and then the other once in 10 s", or "goes through one cycle".

The formulas break across lines ("Xc =" then "1 ÷ 2πfC"; "I = V ÷ Xc =" then "2πfCV") because nb() only binds the space before an operator; keep each formula on one line with a no-wrap span or non-breaking spaces on both sides.

About 170 words of text come before the instruction and the picture, so the control sits well over a screen down; consider putting the picture straight after the first paragraph and the reactance paragraph after the readouts.

findings.where: Screen 4, The why: long cables and the set (WHY_L)
findings.what: "Don't lower the frequency when you don't need to." repeats the sentence before it ("Go lower only when the cable is too big a load..."); cut it.

As a real-job page it lacks the pre-test set check (peak = rms × 1.4142 within the set's kV peak; core µF within the set's rating at the chosen frequency), the terminations check on cables rated above 35 kV, and the full discharge order (display shows discharged, stick, hook, hand earth, earths on core and screen at both ends); only one trap and the Where line touch these.
"IEEE: under 2 up to 3 U0" drops "for installation and acceptance", and IEEE maintenance tests run at about 75% of that, so the card could mislead on a maintenance test; add the qualifier.

findings.where: Screen 12, Keep this case figures and Where line
findings.what: The figure label "VLF test voltage, case cable" uses case-file vocabulary ("String B's VLF test voltage" reads better), and "Where it lives: Run it after..." has a capital letter after the colon.

Points 1 and 4 both say a large capacitance makes a 50 Hz set impractical, and points 1 to 3 are one chain of reasoning, so "any three" can be met by one argument restated; merge 1 and 4 and give the defect-grows-to-failure point its own place so the three needed points are distinct.

A 50 Hz current nobody would test at reads less like a test record than a check that the set can do the job (0.528 µF within 0.75 µF at 0.1 Hz; 107.5 kV peak within 200 kV), which appears only in the after-text; keep 5(c) as the brief set it, but consider making the set check a typed part next time.
